newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lawyers accuse far-right in French graveyard case.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers accuse far-right in French graveyard case.

text.p: Lawyers for French anti-racist groups at the trial of four neo-Nazis accused of desecrating a Jewish cemetery blamed far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen on Wednesday of whipping up anti-Semitism in France.
The accusations, by lawyers for civil plaintiffs, was the latest attempt to link Le Pen's anti-immigrant National Front party to a climate in France that could provoke such attacks.

"If we have the guilty ones, do we have all those responsible?, asked Yann Galut, lawyer for SOS Racisme, in the court. "The one conspicuous by his absence is Jean-Marie Le Pen, the one who made it possible for these men to act."
"Le Pen the words, Carpentras the acts," he added.

The 1990 attack on the centuries-old graveyard in the southern French town of Carpentras, in which the recently buried body of Felix Germon was disinterred and his sodomisation simulated with an umbrella, provoked disgust throughout France and the world.
Le Pen, who has long campaigned to send home three million immigrants, has repeatedly said his extremist party had nothing to do with the attack. He has complained he is the victim of a witchhunt.
The sudden confession last July by one of five desecrators led to the arrest of his alleged accomplices and capped a six-year investigation that had been turning in circles.
Yannick Garnier, 27, Olivier Fimbry, 31, Bertrand Nouveau, 28, and Patrick Laonegro, also 28 and seen as the ideologist of the group, face up to two years in prison if convicted.
A fifth member of the group, Jean-Claude Gos, was killed in a motorcycle accident in December 1993. None were members of the National Front.
Alain Lhote, lawyer for the MRAP anti-racism group, chastised the four defendants as "shaved-heads with empty brains".
"You are Le Pen's offspring, the one who shamelessly crafts words that kill. Who makes this kind of crime morally possible? Le Pen gave them a permit to act, a passport to the indignity," Lhote said.
Anti-racist groups are represented as civil plaintiffs in the trial, seeking to add their weight to the prosecution case.
The descration, in which 34 graves were wrecked, sent hundreds of thousands of people to the streets in a protest march led by late president Francois Mitterrand.

At the time of their arrests, investigators said all four were either members or sympathisers of the tiny Nationalist French and European Party (PNFE) which became known in the late 1980s in connection with a series of attacks on Arab immigrants.
